steps.label: Three-layer perceptron
steps.speakerNotes: Level: undergraduate (year 3). Made from the lecture lec05-kp04 with view-from-text-v3: pages were planned first and each page is mainly one native infographic (designed in HTML and converted to native nodes), with the terms defined on the same page. 10 pages; every number is computed by program.

steps.label: Target codes
steps.speakerNotes: This is the first page of KP04. Prerequisites: codes and cube corners (three lines give three bits, which together name one of the 8 corners), the output layer is one cut (one plane splitting the corners into two sides), and the step rule. At the end of the previous unit A is 000, 110, 111: on the bottom face 000 and 110 are A while 100 and 010 are B, alternating along the diagonal like XOR, so the last layer cannot cut them; 101 is reached by no input. A target code is the code of a corner labelled A. The idea of the fix is not to finish in one cut (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the three steps.

steps.label: Three steps
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the target codes. This page splits the network into three steps: the first hidden layer makes the code with three lines, the second hidden layer holds one detector per target code, and the output layer does an OR merge. A three-layer network means two hidden layers plus an output layer; a detector is a step unit that outputs 1 exactly when the input code equals one target code; an OR merge calls A when any detector outputs 1 and B only when all are 0. The previous unit's two-layer network lacked the detector layer in the middle (computed by program). Next, the next page covers detecting 110.

steps.label: Detecting 110
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the three steps. This page computes a detector's score. For target code t, h equals the sum of s times y over the bits minus (n1 minus 0.5); s is plus 1 where the bit of t is 1 and minus 1 where it is 0, and n1 is the number of 1s in t. Since the sum of s times y equals n1 minus m, with m the number of mismatched bits, h equals 0.5 minus m: a full match scores 0.5, one bit off scores minus 0.5, two off minus 1.5 and three off minus 2.5. For example for 110: y equal to 110 scores 0.5 and 010 scores minus 0.5 (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the three detectors.

steps.label: Three detectors
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on detecting 110. This page applies the same recipe to the three target codes: h000 is minus y1 minus y2 minus y3 plus 0.5; h110 is y1 plus y2 minus y3 minus 1.5; h111 is y1 plus y2 plus y3 minus 2.5. 000 has no 1, so its bias is plus 0.5; 111 has three 1s, so its bias is minus 2.5. The table lists the scores of the three detectors on the eight codes; a positive score appears only at its own corner (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the path through the network.

steps.label: Through the net
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the three detectors. This page substitutes y equal to (1,1,0): the three scores are h000 equal to minus 1.5, h110 equal to 0.5 and h111 equal to minus 0.5; turned into bits b equal to f(h) they give (0,1,0). The output layer adds the bits and subtracts 0.5: 0 plus 1 plus 0 minus 0.5 equals 0.5, above 0, so A. The thick orange lines are the active path (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the OR merge rule.

steps.label: OR merge rule
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the path through the network. This page unifies the merge rule: the output score q is the sum of the three detector bits minus 0.5, that is k minus 0.5, where k is the number of detectors outputting 1. k equal to 0 gives minus 0.5 and B; k at least 1 gives 0.5, 1.5, 2.5 and A. This is the OR merge. The zero lies between k equal to 0 and k equal to 1. Each code fires at most one detector, so only k equal to 0 or 1 occur (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the check of eight corners.

steps.label: Eight corners
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the OR merge rule. This page does not only check the successful inputs but all eight codes. For 010 the three scores are minus 0.5, minus 0.5, minus 1.5, all bits are 0, q is minus 0.5 and the call is B. The unused code 101 also gives all 0 and B; no input reaches it, so classification is unaffected. Only 000, 110, 111 each fire their own detector and are called A (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the input plane.

steps.label: Input plane
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the check of eight corners. This page goes back to the input plane: the three lines g1, g2, g3 cut 8 code regions, the A region is the union of the code regions 000, 110, 111 (110 and 111 are adjacent), and B's 010 is squeezed in between; a single cut cannot do this but the three-layer network does. The three A points and one B point in the figure are all classified right by the program. A common myth is that once a three-layer construction exists the weights have been learned or the network is minimal; the construction only shows it suffices, and how weights come from labelled points is the next unit (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the overlapping rectangles.

steps.label: Overlapping rects
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the input plane. This page is an extension: two overlapping rectangles use 4 lines each, 8 lines in all, to cut the plane into cells; A occupies 7 of them, so 7 detectors are needed, not 2. The number of original rectangles is not the number of codes after refining, and the recipe is unchanged: one detector per code region, then an OR merge (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the exercises.

steps.label: Exercises
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the overlapping rectangles. Two exercises. Q1: 011 has two 1s, weights (minus 1, plus 1, plus 1) and bias minus (2 minus 0.5) equal to minus 1.5, so h011 is minus y1 plus y2 plus y3 minus 1.5; y equal to 011 gives 0 plus 1 plus 1 minus 1.5 equal to 0.5 and y equal to 111 gives minus 1 plus 1 plus 1 minus 1.5 equal to minus 0.5, so 011 outputs 1 and 111 outputs 0. Q2: 010 differs from 011 in one bit, 0.5 minus 1 equals minus 0.5; substituting 0 plus 1 plus 0 minus 1.5 is also minus 0.5, so the two ways agree (computed by program). That ends this unit; next, move on to the next unit.
